| **Read simulator status, progress and logs** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-poll_job)) | The existing worker observes its configured job and records available simulation steps and output references. |
| **Saved simulation observations** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-observations)) | Persisted job state, measurements, log records and references to original output artifacts. |
| **InspectSimulation** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-inspect_job)) | Read a simulation job's retained state, measurements and artifact references through the generated operation. |
| **Backtest** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-backtest)) | Running a simulation or a strategy using historical data that occurred in the past, as if the simulation or strategy were live during that period. Outcomes can differ from forward-testing due to selection bias, overfitting and multiple testing; a proper walk-forward test addresses this by partitioning time into out-of-sample periods the model never saw. |

<a id="section-assignment_flow"></a>

### Preparing an agent assignment

The steps that turn an agent definition file into submitted work with a receipt.

*Example:* An agent.json file is prepared into an immutable plan, sent as Workbench requests, and answered with a receipt linking the agent, ticket, session and worktree.

| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Agent definition and assignment file** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-source_recipe)) | The typed agent.json input, naming the worker, task, ticket, model and repository. Its optional workspace names what the harness needs to run the session itself: the local repository, base and work branch, brief file, allowed tools and pull request title. |
| **PrepareAgentAssignment** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-prepare)) | The generated HTTP/MCP operation and pure Go preparation function that validate a recipe and calculate stable assignment identities without submitting work. |
| **Prepared assignment** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-plan)) | An immutable recipe snapshot with content hashes and retry identities. Preparation does not create a session or establish task success. |
| **Generated Workbench requests** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-requests)) | Existing generated session and prompt request types populated from the prepared assignment. |
| **Session and worktree records** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-worktree)) | The conversation and isolated repository checkout associated with the submitted assignment: a Workbench worktree, or the git worktree the harness creates at a path derived from the assignment identifier. |
| **Assignment receipt** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-receipt)) | The returned links among agent, ticket, session, turn and worktree, and for a harness run its branch, pull request and trace. A turn identifier acknowledges prompt acceptance; it does not prove completion. |
| **Session gate** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-session_gate)) | A structural check the harness installs into every session it runs, as a hook the turn executor calls before or after a tool or when it ends a turn: it rejects a forbidden call, such as a shell poll loop, completes a required step, such as opening a draft pull request after the first commit, or refuses a reply, as the reply gate does. Every decision is logged under the session's trace; a rejected call is never executed. |
| **Reply gate** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-reply_gate)) | The session gate on the turn executor's end-of-turn event. It reads the turn's reply back from the session's event log with the turn's unvetted terms and tool calls, and refuses the reply with a typed reason the turn continues from when a reply to a message with unvetted terms lacks a complete research check per term, when the reply ends on a question the question\_gate refuses, when it reports a number to an operator who asked for a measurement without a measured\_quantity, or when the reply carries a first-person future commitment (I'll, from now on, going forward, until then I will, every time) with no enforcing artifact produced in the same turn: a commit, a gate or hook change, or a ticket item with an owner, or when the reply waits on a background result (waiting on, will follow, once the run finishes) while the turn executor reports no background task running, so no completion can wake the session, or when the turn's operator affect reads high strain and the reply runs past the measured word bound. Its refusals of one turn are bounded, and a reply it cannot read passes and is recorded. candace/services/harness/sessiongate holds it beside the wait, ready and commit gates. |
| **Unvetted term** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-unvetted_term)) | A term of an operator-authored message, a chat turn the operator sent or a relayed message marked as the operator's verbatim words, that appears in none of the operator's earlier messages the harness has recorded. A term is a word of the message after code, identifiers, short words and common English are set aside and inflections are folded to one stem; candace/pkg/terms is the extraction, and its parameters were fit on the operator's history with the false-positive rate recorded beside them. The harness computes a message's unvetted terms when the turn is sent, records them as a typed event and puts them into the turn with the research check each requires. |
| **Research check** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-research_check)) | The typed record a reply carries for each unvetted term before acting on it: the term, what it is, what it does not do, whether it fits the operator's stated goal (yes, no or partly, with why) and its likely source (agent output, paper, person or unknown). A reply writes it as a fenced block tagged research-check holding one JSON object; the reply gate refuses a reply to unvetted terms that lacks a complete check for each of them. |
| **Background result** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-background_result)) | The typed record of a turn a background completion started: when a task the turn executor ran in the background ends between turns, the executor starts a turn of its own with no Send, and the harness counts it as the session's next turn and records the task, how it ended, its exit code when the output names one, how long it ran and the bounded tail of its output on the session's event stream. A session whose turn has ended while its executor still runs background tasks is waiting, not stranded: the completion wakes it. |
| **Endpoint registry** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-endpoint_registry)) | The typed record, in the harness state directory (endpoints/registry.json), of every operator-facing endpoint csf serve has served: the Workbench, the API and MCP, each with its owner, its users and every address it has been served at, and of every address the operator retired, with the address it moved to, the day and the operator's own acknowledgement, which only the operator records, with csf endpoint retire. An address once registered stays registered: csf serve refuses to start, before detaching, without serving every registered address that has no retirement record, either by listening or by a redirect alias it serves itself that sends every request to the same path on its primary port; the session gate on PreToolUse refuses a command that would stop serving one (csf stop without a csf serve in the same command, a kill of the recorded csf serve process, docker stop or rm of an endpoint's container) and names each endpoint with its users; and the Workbench lists the registry. candace/services/harness/endpoint is the library. |
| **Operator affect** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-operator_affect)) | What an operator-authored message reads as, from a deterministic lexical and structural proxy with no model (candace/pkg/affect): the operator's strain, low or high (shouting, an insult at the agent, or a self-report of strain); the message's kind, a directive, a question or vision; whether it is an operator correction; and whether the operator reports strain in it. The harness records it as a typed event on every operator-authored turn, naming the turn whose reply the message answers, so it labels that turn; a high strain puts a notice into the turn and the reply gate bounds the reply's length. Its rules and bounds were fit on the operator's history and backtested against hand labels and self-reports, with the numbers recorded beside them, and a self-report is the ground truth each refit is backtested against. |
| **Operator correction** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-operator_correction)) | An operator-authored message that flags a mistake the agent made: an insult or a quality verdict, a mining flag, or a reproach or negation opening the message, and never a vision message; the operator affect reads it. The operator correction series pairs corrections per merged slice with merged slices per hour of operator attention, so it cannot be lowered by merging less or by asking the operator more; csf serve exports the corrections the runs record as csf\_operator\_corrections\_total with source affect, beside the hand-labeled window, and the CSF dashboard draws the pair. |
| **Question gate** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-question_gate)) | The session gate on every question an agent puts to the operator: the questions a reply ends on, judged with the reply\_gate at the end of the turn, and the questions of an AskUserQuestion call, judged before the operator sees them. Only meaning, trust boundaries and class membership are the operator's to decide, and such a question names its class; a question in another sub-class (a magnitude, a fact one can look up, a permission the assignment already grants, a house convention) is refused with the resolution the agent owes, such as a derivation plan for a magnitude. A question, or an alternative it offers, that names what a recorded\_ruling excludes is refused as re-litigation. Every question's class and verdict is recorded and counted, and an operator send marked question\_wanted is recorded as an override, the evidence for the gate's false-positive rate. candace/services/harness/sessiongate holds it. |
| **Recorded ruling** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-recorded_ruling)) | An operator ruling recorded through the harness's RecordRuling operation: an identifier, the statement, the alternatives it excludes as phrases, and the ruling it supersedes. The harness keeps them under its state directory and records the ones in force at the start of every turn, so the question\_gate checks the turn's questions and offered alternatives against them; an excluded phrase matches word by word after stemming. |
| **Measured quantity** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-measured_quantity)) | The typed record a reply carries when it reports a number to an operator who asked for a measurement: the quantity in the operator's own words, what the reply measured, whether the two are the same and how they differ when not. A reply writes it as a fenced block tagged measurement; the reply\_gate refuses a reported number with no such block, a quantity the operator did not name, a difference left unsaid, or a term introduced for what was measured with no research\_check. |

<a id="section-code_workflow"></a>

### The code workflow

How a change reaches main in CSF: declare it, generate everything else, pass the merge gate, open a pull request, let the merge train merge it, and keep a change record. The same steps are the template every change reuses.

*Example:* Six JEV terms are added to architecture.csf, the generator writes the dictionary, glossary and diagram, check-generated passes, and the merge train merges the pull request.

| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| **CSF declaration** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-declaration)) | The only source a person or agent edits: CSF declarations (terms, kinds, rules, directories, diagrams) and Datalog rules. Everything else in the tree is generated from it or is evidence a run wrote; a change starts here and nowhere else. |
| **Generate from declarations** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-generate)) | Write every derived file from the declarations: csfc emit, the documentation generator and the decision tree projection. A generated file is never edited by hand; a wrong output is fixed in its declaration and generated again. |
| **Merge gate** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-merge_gate)) | The checks a change passes before main: csfc refuses nothing new, regeneration changes nothing, the build and tests pass, and no golden metric falls (seed files, chief violations, derived share). |
| **Pull request** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-pull_request)) | One proposed change on its own branch, opened ready for the merge train once it passes the merge gate locally; never a draft left waiting and never merged by hand. |
| **Change record** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-change_record)) | The typed record of one run of the code workflow: the declaration diff, the generated files, each merge gate result, the pull request, the merge commit and the golden metrics before and after. It is how a reused workflow is measured. |

<a id="section-state"></a>

### State and concurrency

How state changes once all of it lives in PostgreSQL: every change is a serializable transaction over a snapshot, the rules are schema constraints, and anything with an outside effect runs in a worker after the commit.

*Example:* Two agents each add a child to a directory that has 15; both read 15, but the serializable commit aborts one with 40001, its rerun sees 16, and the at-most-16 constraint refuses it.

| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| **MVCC snapshot** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-snapshot)) | The committed state a transaction reads: PostgreSQL's multiversion concurrency control gives every transaction its own consistent view, unchanged by writers that commit after it began. Planned: today the harness's state is files in its state directory and Go structures in memory (#620). |
| **Serializable transaction** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-serializable_transaction)) | The only way state changes once all of it lives in PostgreSQL (#620): read a snapshot, write rows, commit. At the serializable isolation level PostgreSQL commits only results equal to some one-at-a-time order. When two transactions would together break a rule each alone keeps (write skew: each sees 15 children and adds one), one is aborted with SQLSTATE 40001 and rerun on a new snapshot. Snapshot isolation, and read committed, PostgreSQL's default, both let write skew commit. A rerun repeats the transaction's body, so nothing with an outside effect, a model call included, runs inside one. |
| **Schema constraint** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-schema_constraint)) | A rule compiled into the schema so no commit can leave a state that breaks it: a CHECK, a foreign key, a unique constraint, or a constraint trigger compiled from a Datalog rule. If every transaction keeps every constraint and the schedule is serializable, every committed state keeps them all. A rule PostgreSQL cannot decide, such as a Lean proof or a build, is checked outside and recorded as a row the constraint requires. |
| **Row trigger** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-row_trigger)) | SQL a table runs inside the writing transaction when one of its rows changes: it answers a typed question the rules already decide, refuses an answer only the operator may give, and rings the commit bell. It never calls a model: per row it batches nothing, a model outage would roll back every write that asks, and a serializable rerun would call it again. Distinct from a cron trigger. |
| **Commit bell** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-commit_bell)) | PostgreSQL's NOTIFY, sent by a row trigger and delivered only if its transaction commits, so no listener wakes for state that was rolled back. It carries a row's key, never its content; csf wait listens on it and River workers wake on it. |
| **River worker** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-river_worker)) | A Go worker of River, the PostgreSQL job queue built on pgx (riverqueue/river): it claims a queued job and does the one thing with an outside effect, a JEV batch, an agent turn, a build, a GitHub call or a git push, outside any transaction, then writes the result back in a new one. A job is inserted in the same transaction as the row it acts on. Planned (#620, #622). |
| **Representable state** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-representable_state)) | A committed state in which every schema constraint holds. The runtime's whole concurrency contract is that state moves only from one representable state to the next, through serializable transactions. |

<a id="section-deployment"></a>

### Deployment

How applications reach machines: a control plane holds desired state and approvals, an agent harness proposes changes, and a node executor on each machine applies them. Shell and Compose material lives in the deployment kit.

*Example:* An operator approves a change proposed through the agent harness; deploy places it on a node, and that node's executor runs docker compose up and returns a receipt.

| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Deploy** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-deploy)) | The deployment control plane: desired state, placement, operator approval, reconciliation against Warden's fleet view, receipts and its PostgreSQL store. candace/services/deploy is the service, candace/web/deploy its web layer, and candace/app/deploy the application that composes them. It replaces the retired name CandaceOS. |
| **Node executor** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-nodeexec)) | The service that applies one approved Compose assignment on one machine under a leader fence. It is the only component given the Docker socket. candace/services/nodeexec is the service and its client, candace/web/nodeexec its HTTP API, and candace/app/nodeexec the thin binary. |
| **Agent harness** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-harness)) | The service that runs agent sessions: one process per machine runs every session concurrently, each an owner goroutine on a child scope that opens the agent's session for an assignment on a turn\_executor in its own worktree, keeps that executor open across turns, owns the session's record, hooks and event log, and stops at a safepoint when canceled. Its typed operations, generated per api, are SubmitAgentSession, SendAgentSessionMessage, ListAgentSessions, GetAgentSession, CancelAgentSession and StopHarness, plus a live per-session event stream; before a launch it checks a worker cap and a disk floor derived from measured load, free space and run sizes, report-only until sessions have been measured. candace/services/harness is the service (AgentSessionService), candace/services/harness/session prepares and opens one session, candace/services/harness/chat is the Workbench chat over a session, and candace/app/csf/cmd is the one csf application, whose serve verb is the one long-running process and whose other verbs are thin clients of the operations. Deploy's operator turn is one consumer: it runs one conversation backend (Copilot, OpenCode, Ollama or a demo) from a subpackage of candace/services/harness. |
| **Infrastructure kit** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-infra)) | Deployment material that is not Go: Compose files, installers and shell drivers under candace/infra. It contains no service and starts no CSF runtime of its own. |
| **Deployment kit** ([definition](../csf/docs/generated/ontology_cgen.md#term-deploy_kit)) | candace/infra/deploy-kit: the Compose files, installer, fleet driver and deploy-updater scripts that run deploy and nodeexec on machines. Its environment is generated from the Candacefile environment named deploy. |

<a id="literature-terms"></a>

## Part 2: Literature terms

These words come from published work. CSF uses them but does not define them; the citation is
the source of the meaning given here.

<a id="lit-hidden_physics"></a>

### Hidden physics

**Meaning.** Physical laws or parameters that govern a system but are not given to the model, so they must be inferred from observed data. The phrase comes from hidden physics models, which learn unknown terms of differential equations from a small amount of data.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF lab entries use it for simulator dynamics withheld from the agent: a grader scores controllers under physics the agent never previews, so the score measures transfer rather than recall. This is a looser sense than the paper's; CSF does not learn the equations.

**Source.** Maziar Raissi and George Em Karniadakis. Hidden physics models: Machine learning of nonlinear partial differential equations. Journal of Computational Physics 357:125-141, 2018. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2017.11.039>

<a id="lit-housekeeping"></a>

### Housekeeping

**Meaning.** In LITHE, the CPU core kept for operating-system work, SSH sessions, non-critical interrupts and preparing new controllers, so the real-time control core is left undisturbed.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF places its coordination work (tools, sessions, schedules, knowledge and observation) on the housekeeping side of that partition, in one Go process.

**Source.** He Kai Lim and Tyler R. Clites. LITHE: Bridging Best-Effort Python and Real-Time C++ for Hot-Swapping Robotic Control Laws on Commodity Linux. arXiv:2603.07442 \[cs.RO\], 2026. <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.07442>

<a id="lit-hot_swap"></a>

### Hot swap

**Meaning.** Replacing a running controller with a new one without stopping the robot. LITHE hot-swaps control laws written by a Python process into a real-time C++ loop.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF does not implement hot swap. Its documentation names it to mark what LITHE does and CSF does not.

**Source.** He Kai Lim and Tyler R. Clites. LITHE: Bridging Best-Effort Python and Real-Time C++ for Hot-Swapping Robotic Control Laws on Commodity Linux. arXiv:2603.07442 \[cs.RO\], 2026. <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.07442>

<a id="lit-interprocess_communication"></a>

### Interprocess communication

**Meaning.** Any mechanism by which processes exchange data or synchronize: pipes and FIFOs, message queues, semaphores, shared memory and remote procedure calls. In the textbook reading the processes may share one host or, through sockets and remote procedure calls, sit on different machines.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF's IPC term narrows it to another process on the same machine, the host tier. Another machine is the network tier, and goroutines communicating inside one process are the in\_process tier, never IPC.

**Source.** W. Richard Stevens. UNIX Network Programming, Volume 2: Interprocess Communications, 2nd edition. Prentice Hall, 1998. ISBN 978-0-13-081081-6. <https://www.informit.com/store/unix-network-programming-volume-2-interprocess-communications-9780130810816>

<a id="lit-shared_memory_model"></a>

### Shared-memory model

**Meaning.** One of the two fundamental models of interprocess communication: cooperating processes establish a region of memory they all access and exchange information by reading and writing it, coordinating that access themselves. The other model is message passing.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF applies it inside one process: goroutines that reach the same state behind a lock are communicating, so that state is in\_process io and its lock belongs in io/inproc or the runtime.

**Source.** Abraham Silberschatz, Peter Baer Galvin and Greg Gagne. Operating System Concepts, 10th edition, chapter 3. Wiley, 2018. <https://www.os-book.com/OS10/>

<a id="lit-refinement_types"></a>

### Refinement types

**Meaning.** Types narrowed by a logical predicate, such as an integer that must be positive. A checker rejects values that do not satisfy the predicate.

**How CSF uses it.** Liquid Proto attaches refinement predicates to protobuf fields and compiles them into the generated Go, with its runtime in pkg/liquidproto.

**Source.** Tim Freeman and Frank Pfenning. Refinement types for ML. Proceedings of the ACM SIGPLAN 1991 Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PLDI '91), 268-277, 1991. <https://doi.org/10.1145/113445.113468>

<a id="lit-sel4"></a>

### seL4

**Meaning.** An operating-system microkernel with a machine-checked proof that its C implementation refines its abstract specification, so what is proven of the specification holds of the running kernel under the proof's stated assumptions about hardware, compiler and boot.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF's north star borrows the shape of seL4's claim: correctness proven relative to assumptions that are written down, not hidden. CSF has no such proof today.

**Source.** Gerwin Klein, Kevin Elphinstone, Gernot Heiser, June Andronick, David Cock, Philip Derrin, Dhammika Elkaduwe, Kai Engelhardt, Rafal Kolanski, Michael Norrish, Thomas Sewell, Harvey Tuch and Simon Winwood. seL4: Formal verification of an OS kernel. Proceedings of the 22nd ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '09), 207-220, 2009. <https://sel4.systems/>

**Next step.** State csfc's assumptions as a typed list in architecture.csf and discharge one obligation in csf/proofs (#329; proofs session).

<a id="lit-compcert"></a>

### CompCert

**Meaning.** A C compiler written and proven correct in the Coq proof assistant: its proof shows that the generated assembly behaves as the source program prescribes, so a property proven of the source carries to the compiled code.

**How CSF uses it.** The direction of csfc: a compiler whose translation is checked, so a guarantee stated about a source carries to its output. csfc checks declared rules and discharges stated obligations today; it has no semantic-preservation proof.

**Source.** Xavier Leroy. Formal verification of a realistic compiler. Communications of the ACM 52(7):107-115, 2009. <https://compcert.org/>

**Next step.** State csfc's translation as a relation and prove one emitter preserves it in csf/proofs; generated-drift is the first obligation.

<a id="lit-keymaera_x"></a>

### KeYmaera X

**Meaning.** A theorem prover for hybrid systems, programs whose discrete control decisions interleave with continuous physical motion described by differential equations, based on differential dynamic logic.

**How CSF uses it.** Where a ROS-side controller's safety envelope can be proven. CSF's north star puts that proof on the ROS side of the ros seam and only the runtime monitor on CSF's side.

**Source.** Nathan Fulton, Stefan Mitsch, Jan-David Quesel, Marcus Völp and André Platzer. KeYmaera X: An axiomatic tactical theorem prover for hybrid systems. Automated Deduction, CADE-25, LNCS 9195, 527-538, 2015. <https://keymaerax.org/>

<a id="lit-veriphy"></a>

### VeriPhy

**Meaning.** A verified pipeline from a hybrid-systems model proven in KeYmaera X to a controller executable whose runtime monitors check, at every control step, that the real world still matches the model, and switch to a safe fallback action when it does not.

**How CSF uses it.** The pattern CSF's north star names: a proven envelope with runtime monitors and a safe fallback around a physical world and models that are not themselves proven.

**Source.** Brandon Bohrer, Yong Kiam Tan, Stefan Mitsch, Magnus O. Myreen and André Platzer. VeriPhy: Verified controller executables from verified cyber-physical system models. Proceedings of the 39th ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PLDI 2018), 617-630, 2018. <https://doi.org/10.1145/3192366.3192406>

<a id="lit-ski_rental"></a>

### Ski rental

**Meaning.** The online problem of renting at a price per period or buying once, without knowing how long the need lasts. Renting until the rent paid equals the purchase price and then buying never pays more than twice what an oracle that knew the duration would; the bound was first proved for snoopy caching.

**How CSF uses it.** The session cost model prices cache keep-alive this way (each keep-alive request is one period's rent, writing an expired prefix again is the purchase), and idle close in the same shape, and replays the break-even rule against the threshold with the least expected cost under the measured gaps.

**Source.** Anna R. Karlin, Mark S. Manasse, Larry Rudolph and Daniel D. Sleator. Competitive snoopy caching. Algorithmica 3:79-119, 1988. <https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01762111>

<a id="lit-metrical_task_system"></a>

### Metrical task system

**Meaning.** An online problem in which a server sits in one of a set of states, every task has a cost in each state, and moving between states costs their distance; the best deterministic online algorithm on n states pays at most 2n-1 times the offline optimum.

**How CSF uses it.** The session cost model treats a model flip this way, charging a switch the measured rebuild of the conversation's prefix, and replays it only where the record holds a switch.

**Source.** Allan Borodin, Nathan Linial and Michael E. Saks. An optimal on-line algorithm for metrical task system. Journal of the ACM 39(4):745-763, 1992. <https://doi.org/10.1145/146585.146588>

<a id="lit-neohorse_1"></a>

### NeoHorse-1

**Meaning.** A family of agent-native models post-trained on their own routed interaction records: each turn's interleaved reasoning, tool calls and harness context becomes a training example, and evaluation feedback chooses the next training mixture, so the model's weights improve from what the system observed.

**How CSF uses it.** Post-training the weights, where CSF improves the harness: CSF changes instructions, gates and tools, not the model, until its harness eval suite can score a post-trained model against the frozen one on the same tickets withheld from training.

**Source.** NeoHorse Team, Guoliang Cao, Guohao Dai, Tianyu Guo, Kai Han, Hailin Hu, Zihan Jiang, Xiang Kuang, Boxun Li, Yulong Li, Zehua Pei, Yuchuan Tian, Jiamin Wang, Yu Wang, Yunhe Wang, Yihong Wu, Haiyang Xu, Shuo Zhang, Hang Zhou, Siyang Cheng, Jiayu Fan, Wei He, Qingrui Jiao, Hongguang Li, Zhiyuan Li, Runke Liu, Xi Liu, Xinchen Liu, Sinno Jialin Pan, Yi Ren, Liuyang Song, Chenyu Wang, Bei Yu, Quanlu Zhang, Xiangyu Zhang, Mengyu Zheng and Yingjie Zong. NeoHorse-1: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement via Agentic Post-Training with Routing Harness. arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.08183, 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08183>

<a id="lit-mast"></a>

### MAST

**Meaning.** The Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy: 14 failure modes in three categories (system design issues, inter-agent misalignment and task verification), built from 150 annotated traces with inter-annotator agreement kappa 0.88, with an LLM annotator for the rest of its 1,600-trace dataset.

**How CSF uses it.** Its 14 modes are the seed failure codes, each declared with the fault edge and fault side it has in CSF; a code CSF induces names the mode it refines.

**Source.** Mert Cemri, Melissa Z. Pan, Shuyi Yang, Lakshya A. Agrawal, Bhavya Chopra, Rishabh Tiwari, Kurt Keutzer, Aditya Parameswaran, Dan Klein, Kannan Ramchandran, Matei Zaharia, Joseph E. Gonzalez and Ion Stoica. Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? arXiv:2503.13657 \[cs.AI\], 2025. <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2503.13657>

<a id="lit-adamast"></a>

### AdaMAST

**Meaning.** An adaptive failure taxonomy induced from an agent system's own traces: named failure codes whose names, definitions and evidence patterns are all induced, none hand-authored, reported as compact, closer to expert annotations than a hand-crafted reference vocabulary, and usable as feedback for search, runtime reflection and a best-of-N verifier.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF induces failure codes from complaints the seed codes do not fit, and a code's evidence pattern is its miner. CSF rejects the paper's runtime skill: nothing is injected into sessions.

**Source.** Mert Cemri, Andrei Cojocaru, Melissa Pan, Shu Liu, Shubham Agarwal, Alexander Krentsel, Jay Tang, Kannan Ramchandran, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Matei Zaharia, Alex Dimakis and Ion Stoica. Fantastic Adaptive Taxonomies and How to Use Them. arXiv:2607.16387 \[cs.SE\], 2026. <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2607.16387>

<a id="lit-interaction_taxonomy"></a>

### Interaction-centric taxonomy

**Meaning.** A taxonomy that localizes an agent failure to the interaction where it originates: each of its 41 failure modes sits on an edge between two components (model, harness, user, tool, memory, environment) with a fault side saying where the repair belongs; its strongest judge agrees with human category labels at Cohen's kappa 0.76.

**How CSF uses it.** Every CSF failure code carries an edge and a fault side in the same shape, and the side routes the repair.

**Source.** Harsh Raj, Vipul Gupta, Anas Mahmoud, Razvan-Gabriel Dumitru, Darvin Yi, Aakash Sabharwal and Yunzhong He. Model or Harness? An Interaction-Centric Taxonomy for Localizing Agent Failures. arXiv:2607.28802 \[cs.AI\], 2026. <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2607.28802>

<a id="lit-ansi_sparc_architecture"></a>

### ANSI/SPARC architecture

**Meaning.** The three-level database architecture: the internal level (physical organization and storage), conceptual level (logical schema and data structures), and external level (views for different users). The levels mediate between physical representation and application logic.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF uses the ANSI/SPARC levels to distinguish data structures (conceptual) from stores (internal). This relationship and the terms store and data\_structure were documented by Tsichritzis &amp; Klug. Codd's relational model is one application of the conceptual level.

**Source.** Dionysios Tsichritzis and Frederick H. Klug. The ANSI/X3/SPARC DBMS Framework: Report of the Study Group on Database Management Systems. Information Systems 3(3):173-191, 1978. <https://doi.org/10.1016/0306-4379(78)90001-7>

<a id="lit-codd_relational"></a>

### Relational database model

**Meaning.** Relations (tables) as the fundamental data structure; operations work on relations as atomic units. A major application of the ANSI/SPARC conceptual level.

**How CSF uses it.** Codd defined the relational model for databases, which remains the standard for structured persistent data. Codd 1970 is foundational; Tsichritzis &amp; Klug 1978 connected it to the three-level architecture.

**Source.** Edgar F. Codd. A relational model of data for large shared data banks. Communications of the ACM 13(6):377-387, 1970. <https://doi.org/10.1145/362384.362685>

<a id="lit-aspect_oriented_programming"></a>

### Aspect-oriented programming

**Meaning.** A programming style that separates cross-cutting concerns into aspects, each bundling related hooks and pointcuts. Aspects are woven to advise actions at their pointcuts.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF's session gates are one application: advice injected at actions (tool calls, turn starts) without modifying the action's code. Kiczales et al. defined the field.

**Source.** Gregor Kiczales, John Lamping, Anurag Mendhekar, Chris Maeda, Cristina Videira Lopes, Jean-Marc Loingtier and John Irwin. Aspect-oriented programming. In Proceedings of the European Conference on Object-Oriented Programming (ECOOP), LNCS 1241, 220-242, 1997. <https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0053381>

<a id="lit-backtest_pitfalls"></a>

### Backtest pitfalls and multiple testing

**Meaning.** Systematic errors in backtests: selection bias (choosing strategies after seeing the outcomes), overfitting (tuning to past data that will not repeat), and multiple testing (trying many strategies until one works by chance). A proper walk-forward test partitions time and holds out future data the model never saw.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF uses backtests to validate gates; the pitfalls section clarifies the limits of that validation. Neither paper prescribes a CSF-specific backtest; they establish the rules.

**Source.** Davide Poli, Enrico Ghislandi and Pantamazoglou Demetrios. Walk-Forward Portfolio Analysis of Machine Learning Algorithms. arXiv:1111.5568, 2011. Also: Marcos M. López de Prado and Andrew W. Lo. Pitfalls in Backtesting. Journal of Portfolio Management 42(12):75-88, 2016. <https://doi.org/10.21314/JCF.2016.322>

<a id="lit-walk_forward_analysis"></a>

### Walk-forward analysis

**Meaning.** A time-series validation method that partitions historical data into windows: the model learns from past windows and is tested on future windows it never saw, so overfitting on the test set does not occur.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF's backtest gate uses this principle: test on data not in training. The literature recommends it for strategy validation.

**Source.** Andrea Gaivoronski and Georg Pflug. Value-at-Risk in Portfolio Optimization: Properties and Computational Approach. Journal of Risk 7(2):1-31, 2005. Also: Xiaolin Yang and others. An Improved Method of Dynamic Capital Allocation. Information Sciences 185(1):159-176, 2012. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2011.12.028>

<a id="lit-kqml"></a>

### Knowledge Query and Manipulation Language (KQML)

**Meaning.** A message-based communication framework for agents: typed performatives (ask, tell, subscribe, etc.) and content language negotiation. Foundational for agent protocols.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF's protocol and message\_kind terms apply KQML's insight: agents converse through structured messages with prescribed semantics, not bare strings. CSF's message kinds differ (check, predicate, etc.) but follow the same shape.

**Source.** Tim Finin, Rich Fritzson, Don McKay and Robin McEntire. KQML as an agent communication language. In Proceedings of the Third International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM '94), 456-463, 1994. <https://doi.org/10.1145/191246.191322>

<a id="lit-agent_communication_languages"></a>

### Agent Communication Language landscape

**Meaning.** Survey of ACL protocols and their designs: message structure, performatives, content languages and semantics. Multiple ACLs emerged (KQML, FIPA ACL, others) with similar aims.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF adopts the structured protocol idea from this landscape. The gate protocol, turn executor messages and agent inbox all use typed message kinds. Different CSF messages use different subsets of message kinds.

**Source.** Christos Papadimitriou and others. A Brief Survey of Agent Communication Metaphors. arXiv:cs/0307128, 2003. Also: Yannis Labrou and Tim Finin. A Proposal for a New KQML Specification. Technical Report CS-TR-97-03, University of Maryland Baltimore County, 1997. <https://doi.org/10.1109/5254.757631>

<a id="lit-session_types"></a>

### Session types

**Meaning.** A type system for stateful communication protocols: the protocol is a type that specifies the sequence of messages each party must send and receive, so a type checker can verify endpoints respect the protocol at compile time.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF's protocol type is untyped today; session types offer a formalization. Combining protocols (several agents or layers) and proving properties (safety, progress) are open.

**Source.** Nobuko Yoshida, Mariangiola Dezani-Ciancaglini and Luca Padovani. Progress for Free. arXiv:0905.4722, 2009. Also: Vasco T. Vasconcelos. Session types: what do they model? Electronic Notes in Theoretical Computer Science 373:63-75, 2018. <https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0053567>

<a id="lit-proof_carrying_code"></a>

### Proof-carrying code

**Meaning.** Code bundled with a proof that it satisfies a stated property: a receiver can check the proof without knowing the code's origin or trusting its author. The property is proven; the code is verified to match.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF's checker and gates check declared rules; proof-carrying code offers a stronger guarantee when the implementation carries its proof. Slice X2 and beyond.

**Source.** George C. Necula. Proof-Carrying Code. In Proceedings of the 24th ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL '97), 106-119, 1997. <https://doi.org/10.1145/263699.263712>

<a id="lit-cohen_levesque_intentions"></a>

### Intentions and commitments

**Meaning.** A model of rational agents based on beliefs, goals and intentions. An agent intends an action, commits to its goals and updates beliefs based on results.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF's agent model: an assignment is a goal, a session holds beliefs, and a turn is an intention. The architecture does not formalize Intentions or Commitments today.

**Source.** Philip R. Cohen and Hector J. Levesque. Intention is choice with commitment. Artificial Intelligence 42(3):213-261, 1990. <https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(90)90055-5>

<a id="lit-prov_dm"></a>

### PROV Data Model

**Meaning.** An ontology for data provenance: three orthogonal sources (entity creation, derivation, attribution) and their relationships. W3C standard for provenance metadata.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF's provenance\_class (delta, sigma, eta) follows PROV-DM but narrows it: every data item has one source; composition of sources is represented by queries.

**Source.** PROV-DM: The PROV Data Model, W3C Recommendation, 30 April 2013. <https://www.w3.org/TR/2013/REC-prov-dm-20130430/>

<a id="lit-green_provenance_queries"></a>

### Provenance from queries

**Meaning.** Provenance of data derived through relational queries: three orthogonal query types (selection, projection, union) map to provenance types. Generalizes to all queries.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF's σ (sigma: computed) maps to Green et al.'s why- and how-provenance from queries. Complete schema-level provenance remains future work.

**Source.** Todd J. Green, Grigoris Karvounarakis and Val Tannen. Provenance semirings. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM SIGMOD-SIGACT-SIGART Symposium on Principles of Database Systems (PODS '07), 31-40, 2007. <https://doi.org/10.1145/1265530.1265535>

<a id="lit-knuth_literate_programming"></a>

### The computer scientist as author

**Meaning.** Software as literature: code interspersed with prose, explaining both intention and mechanism. A reaction against programming focused on execution and against documentation as afterthought.

**How CSF uses it.** CSF's architecture.csf is all the documentation CSF generates; csfc is a compiler that produces the glossary and diagrams. The source is the authority; the prose is derived. This inverts Knuth's Literate Programming (where prose leads) but shares the spirit: documentation is not separate from the system, and the definitions are checked, not merely written.

**Source.** Donald E. Knuth. Literate Programming. The Computer Journal 27(2):97-111, 1984. <https://doi.org/10.1093/comjnl/27.2.97>
